questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. BP is now 82/54 mm Hg, HR 124/min, and heart sounds are muffled.
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate while the patient is deteriorating? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: New hemodynamic instability with an effusion warrants immediate escalation, monitoring, and a focused handoff.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Activate the facility’s emergency response
Continue bedside monitoring of blood pressure and heart rate
Communicate the known effusion and new hypotension
Send the patient to routine imaging alone
Delay escalation until the next scheduled vital signs

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. The nurse has assessed the patient and the response team is available. This exercise follows the facility’s escalation pathway. Actions within a step may occur concurrently.
questions.stem: Place the escalation milestones in order.
questions.rationale: Escalation brings the team to the bedside, where the focused handoff informs urgent evaluation and subsequent reassessment.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Assist with the team’s urgent bedside evaluation
Activate the emergency response at the bedside
Trend hemodynamics after the team intervenes
Give the responding team the vital-sign trend and known effusion

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. The bedside echocardiogram shows right-sided chamber collapse during filling.
questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains the falling blood pressure?
questions.rationale: Compression limits filling, reducing stroke volume and cardiac output.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling
Fluid raises end-diastolic volume
Systemic vascular resistance falls from isolated vasodilation
Ventricular filling rises as external pressure increases

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. The team documents cardiac tamponade.
questions.stem: Which type of shock is caused by this mechanical impairment of filling?
questions.rationale: External compression obstructs filling despite blood being available to return to the heart.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Obstructive
Distributive
Hypovolemic
Neurogenic

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. The team relieves the pericardial pressure and asks the nurse to reassess.
questions.stem: Which two trends most directly support improved circulation? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Improved filling can increase stroke volume, blood pressure, and pulse strength.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Blood pressure rises
Previously weak peripheral pulses become stronger
Heart rate accelerates while pressure falls
Mental status deteriorates
Peripheral pulses become harder to detect

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. After initial improvement, the patient again becomes hypotensive and tachycardic.
questions.stem: Which interpretation should guide the nurse’s report?
questions.rationale: Recurrent hypotension and tachycardia are deterioration cues, even after initial improvement.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Recurrent hemodynamic compromise requires immediate reassessment
Initial improvement rules out recurrent compromise
Tachycardia establishes adequate cardiac output
The earlier effusion makes the blood pressure trend irrelevant

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. The nurse compares the earlier effusion with the later bedside assessment.
questions.stem: Match each term to its defining feature.
questions.rationale: These terms describe the fluid, the resulting compression, and the perfusion consequence.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

targets.text: Inadequate perfusion from mechanical obstruction to circulation

questions.caseText: A 57-year-old recovering from cardiac surgery reports worsening breathlessness. An earlier echocardiogram showed fluid in the pericardial sac. At handoff, the nurse is asked why an earlier stable effusion became urgent.
questions.stem: Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.rationale: The hemodynamic effect determines urgency. An effusion can become critical when pressure limits filling.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: The urgency changed when signs of impaired cardiac filling and perfusion appeared
Any amount of pericardial fluid causes the same hemodynamic effect
Fluid around the heart improves filling until it enters a ventricle
The concern depends solely on the size of the effusion

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. The patient is pale and dizzy. BP fell from 116/72 to 86/50 mm Hg and HR rose to 122/min.
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate now? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Active hematemesis with hypotension and tachycardia warrants urgent assessment and escalation.

options.text: Activate the emergency response
Stay with the patient and reassess airway and circulation
Report the volume and appearance of emesis and the vital-sign changes
Give oral fluids while vomiting continues
Delay escalation until the next scheduled assessment

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. A colleague is available to assist. Use the unit’s escalation pathway. Actions within a step may occur concurrently.
questions.stem: Place the milestones in order.
questions.rationale: Activation and handoff precede team-directed stabilization and subsequent reassessment.

options.text: Assist with the team’s ordered stabilization and source evaluation
Activate the emergency response for active bleeding and instability
Reassess circulation and watch for recurrent bleeding
Give the team the bleeding history and vital-sign trend

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. After initial stabilization, endoscopy identifies bleeding esophageal varices.
questions.stem: What led to the formation of the varices?
questions.rationale: Portal hypertension diverts blood into collateral veins that can enlarge and bleed.

options.text: Portal blood was diverted through fragile collateral veins
Albumin increased pressure inside esophageal arteries
Bile obstruction increased flow into esophageal veins
Pancreatic enzymes weakened the esophageal lining

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. The team asks why the patient lost circulating volume so quickly.
questions.stem: Which explanation best fits the bleeding source?
questions.rationale: Ruptured varices can cause substantial upper GI blood loss.

options.text: Dilated thin-walled veins can rupture and bleed into the upper GI tract
Ascites alone transfers blood directly into the stomach
Low albumin causes bleeding by increasing clotting-factor synthesis
Esophageal collateral formation prevents blood loss when a vein ruptures

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. After bleeding control, abdominal distention persists. Albumin is below the laboratory’s reference range.
questions.stem: Which two mechanisms explain the ongoing ascites? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Portal hypertension promotes filtration, while low albumin reduces the force retaining water in vessels.

options.text: Higher portal hydrostatic pressure
Lower plasma oncotic pressure
Increased plasma albumin
Reduced portal pressure
Increased fluid return to the circulation

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. After circulation stabilizes, the patient becomes inattentive and develops a flapping hand tremor.
questions.stem: Which complication should the nurse report as a concern?
questions.rationale: New cognitive change with asterixis is consistent with hepatic encephalopathy and needs reassessment.

options.text: Hepatic encephalopathy
Uncomplicated ascites alone
Isolated low albumin without neurologic effects
Uncomplicated reflux

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. At handoff the nurse reviews the pathophysiology behind several findings.
questions.stem: Match each finding to its mechanism.
questions.rationale: These findings arise from altered portal flow, reduced protein synthesis, or both.

targets.text: Portal blood is diverted through collateral veins
Portal pressure and reduced oncotic pressure promote fluid accumulation

questions.caseText: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and ascites suddenly vomits bright red blood on the inpatient unit. The patient has no further visible hematemesis, but BP falls and HR rises again.
questions.stem: Which response best addresses this change?
questions.rationale: Recurrent hemodynamic deterioration warrants urgent reassessment, even without visible emesis.

options.text: Escalate immediately for recurrent bleeding or another cause of shock
Assume bleeding has stopped permanently because no blood is visible
Attribute the trend to stable ascites and wait
Use a low albumin result alone to rule out recurrent bleeding

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. Glucose is 412 mg/dL. The patient is tachycardic and has dry mucous membranes.
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate during the initial evaluation? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The patient needs prompt evaluation of perfusion, neurologic status, ketones, and electrolytes. Glucose alone cannot distinguish DKA from other causes of hyperglycemia.

options.text: Repeat and trend vital signs and mental status
Report the missed insulin and breathing pattern to the care team
Obtain ordered ketone and electrolyte testing
Use glucose alone to decide whether ketoacidosis is present
Delay escalation until vomiting resolves

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. DKA is confirmed. The IV is ready, the isotonic fluid order can start immediately, and the potassium result is pending. The insulin order requires potassium verification. The monitoring schedule specifies repeat labs during treatment.
questions.stem: Place the protocol milestones in order.
questions.rationale: The specified protocol addresses volume loss and checks potassium before insulin, then tracks response.

options.text: Start insulin per the protocol
Start the ordered isotonic fluid
Trend repeat glucose, electrolytes and ketones during treatment
Verify potassium meets the protocol’s threshold for insulin

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. Before insulin, arterial pH is 7.21, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L and PaCO₂ 25 mm Hg. Reference ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, bicarbonate 22–26 mEq/L and PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg.
questions.stem: Which interpretation explains the breathing pattern?
questions.rationale: Low pH and bicarbonate support metabolic acidosis. Deep rapid breathing reduces PaCO₂.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis with a compensatory fall in PaCO₂
Primary respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with a compensatory rise in PaCO₂
Primary respiratory alkalosis with normal bicarbonate

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. Glucose is elevated and blood ketones are markedly elevated.
questions.stem: Which process produced the ketones?
questions.rationale: When insulin is severely deficient, fatty acids from lipolysis provide substrate for hepatic ketogenesis.

options.text: Severe insulin deficiency promoted fat breakdown and hepatic ketone production
Excess insulin promoted lipolysis
The kidney converted urinary glucose directly into ketones
ADH stimulated ketone production

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. Glucose has fallen during treatment, but ketones remain elevated.
questions.stem: Which two trends best establish improvement in ketoacidosis itself? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Ketones and acid-base status indicate improvement in DKA. A lower glucose alone does not establish resolution.

options.text: Blood ketones decline
Bicarbonate rises toward the reference range
Glucose falls with no change in acid-base status
Urine glucose is still detectable
The patient reports thirst with no lab reassessment

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. The nurse compares this episode with a case of HHS.
questions.stem: Which finding in this patient most strongly favors DKA?
questions.rationale: Significant ketonemia with metabolic acidosis distinguishes DKA from typical HHS. Both can cause severe dehydration.

options.text: Marked ketone elevation with metabolic acidosis
Dehydration with tachycardia
Glucosuria
Elevated serum glucose

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. During recovery, the patient asks why the missed doses mattered during illness.
questions.stem: Which teaching response explains the risk?
questions.rationale: Illness can increase metabolic stress. A sick-day plan addresses insulin, monitoring, and when to seek help.

options.text: Illness can increase insulin needs, and inadequate insulin allows ketone production
Vomiting eliminates the need for insulin until eating resumes
A lower glucose reading guarantees ketone production has stopped
Ketones are caused by taking prescribed insulin during illness

questions.caseText: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, excessive thirst, and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin during an illness. The nurse uses teach-back to review the findings during admission.
questions.stem: Match each finding to the process it reflects.
questions.rationale: These findings reflect urinary water loss, respiratory compensation, and altered fuel use.

targets.text: Insulin deficiency promotes fat breakdown and ketone production
Increased ventilation helps compensate for metabolic acidosis
Glucose in the filtrate promotes osmotic diuresis
